modules.title: Calculation: the Aagaard toolkit
modules.summary: Five habits of strong calculators: list every forcing candidate, compare similar lines, eliminate what fails, check for intermediate moves and desperadoes, and look for the quiet move at the end of a line.
modules.source: Aagaard, Grandmaster Preparation: Calculation (candidate moves, combinational vision, comparison, elimination, intermediate moves, imagination); Yusupov, Boost Your Chess 3 (ch. 15 candidate moves, ch. 16 combinational vision, ch. 23 the elimination method) and Chess Evolution 3 (ch. 1 desperadoes, ch. 3 the comparison method); model games Botvinnik–Capablanca 1938, Kasparov–Topalov 1999, Lasker–Napier 1904, Réti–Bogoljubov 1924, Short–Timman 1991

lessons.title: Candidate moves and combinational vision
lessons.objective: Put every forcing move on your candidate list, including the sacrifice that looks impossible, before you calculate any of them.

sections.md:
Aagaard's finding from thousands of training positions: strong players rarely miss a win because they calculate it badly. They miss it because the winning move never reached their list of candidates.

So build the list before you calculate:

1. Every check, capture and threat, for both sides.
2. Every move that attacks the squares around the enemy king.
3. The moves that look impossible: a piece put where it can be taken, a sacrifice on a defended square, a quiet move that ignores a threat.

Combinational vision is the pattern half of the skill. Look for a piece that does two jobs, a king without a flight square, a pawn one step from promotion. When you see one, ask which move exploits it, even if that move gives away a piece.

Then calculate, most forcing line first. Botvinnik–Capablanca, AVRO 1938, is the classic test: every natural move keeps an edge, and the winning move puts a bishop where the queen can take it.

sections.caption: Botvinnik–Capablanca, move 30, White to play. The queen on e7 has two jobs: she stops the e6-pawn and she guards the knight on f6. A piece with two jobs is a target.

sections.question: Which candidate attacks the overloaded piece?
options: 30.h4, gaining space on the kingside
30.Ba3, attacking the queen
30.Ne2, bringing the knight to d4 or f4
sections.explanation: 30.Ba3!! is Botvinnik's move, and it attacks the overloaded queen. 30...Qxa3 loses to the combination in the next challenge. 30...Qe8, the best defence, gives the pawn the e7-square and White keeps a winning attack (Stockfish +3.3). 30.h4 is also strong (+2.6 at depth 21 against +3.1 for 30.Ba3), but it gives Black a tempo and does not touch the overloaded queen.

sections.prompt: Capablanca took the bishop: 30...Qxa3. White to play. The queen has left e7. Find the move that wins.
sections.hint: The knight on f6 is the last guard of e8. First remove the pawn that shields the black king.
sections.explanation: 31.Nh5+! gxh5 32.Qg5+ and 33.Qxf6+ wins the knight with check; then the e-pawn cannot be stopped. The game went 32...Kf8 33.Qxf6+ Kg8 34.e7 and Black resigned on move 41 after running out of checks. Stockfish rates 31.Nh5+ at +5.5; the next move, 31.Qc7+, only draws.

sections.prompt: Petrosian–Spassky, World Championship 1966, game 10. White to play. Nothing guards the black queen on g5, and only the king guards the rook on f7. Find the combination.
sections.hint: A queen sacrifice with check drags the king onto a square where a knight fork works.
sections.explanation: 30.Qh8+!! Kxh8 31.Nxf7+ Kg7 32.Nxg5. The knight takes the rook with check and then the queen. White ends a piece up (Stockfish +6.1). The candidate that looks impossible, a queen move to a square guarded by the king, is the only winning one; 30.Nxf7 wins less than a pawn's worth.

lessons.title: The comparison method
lessons.objective: When two candidates lead to similar positions, put the lines side by side and find the one detail that decides between them.

sections.caption: Kasparov–Topalov after 24...cxd4. Two candidates with the same pieces: the queen check on d4 and the rook check on e7.

sections.question: Compare 25.Qxd4+ and 25.Re7+. Why does only the rook check first work?
options: After 25.Qxd4+ Black blocks with 25...Qb6 and offers a queen trade; after 25.Re7+ the queen cannot take the rook, because 25...Qxe7 26.Qxd4+ leads to mate.
Because 25.Qxd4+ loses the queen to a knight fork.
There is no difference: both checks win, Kasparov just chose one.
sections.explanation: Same pieces, different order. 25.Qxd4+? Qb6! blocks the check with a queen trade offer, and Black is better (Stockfish about -1.8). 25.Re7+! comes first, and now the d6-queen is overloaded: 25...Qxe7 26.Qxd4+ Qc5 27.Qxc5+ Kb8 28.Qb6+ Bb7 29.Qxb7#. One detail decides: in one order the black queen reaches b6 in time, in the other she is needed on e7.

sections.prompt: Now play it, in the right order. White to move.
sections.hint: Rook check first; then the queen takes on d4, also with check.
sections.explanation: 25.Re7+! Kb6 26.Qxd4+. In the game Topalov went 26...Kxa5 27.b4+ Ka4, and the king was pulled among the white pawns. Each check gains the tempo that the other move order would have lost.

lessons.title: The elimination method
lessons.objective: When the best move cannot be calculated to the end, prove that every other move loses and play the one that remains.

sections.md:
Some positions cannot be calculated to the end. The elimination method does not try. List the candidate moves, refute each one with a concrete line, and play the move that is left. You do not need to prove that it wins. You only need to prove that the others lose.

The method is strongest in defence and in critical positions, where most moves lose by force. Aagaard calls these critical decisions: the gap between the best move and the second-best is large, so it pays to spend time.

Two rules:

1. Refute each rejected move with a real line, not a feeling. A move you rejected without a reason may be the only one.
2. Keep the refutations short. A check, a fork or a mate in two is enough.

Kasparov–Topalov again, move 36. The black king has run to d1. Black's queen and rooks threaten mate, and almost every White move loses. One does not.

sections.caption: Move 36, White to play. If White passes, 36...Qd3+ 37.Ka1 Ra8+ mates (Stockfish: mate in five). The candidates must meet that threat.

sections.prompt: White to play. Eliminate the moves that lose, then play the one that is left and follow it up.
sections.hint: Which piece can attack the queen and cover d3 at the same time? Then a rook offer deflects the d8-rook.
sections.explanation: 36.Bf1!! attacks the queen and covers d3. 36...Rd2 is Black's best try (Stockfish, depth 22). 37.Rd7!! Rxd7 38.Bxc4 bxc4 39.Qxh8, and White ends with queen against rook. Every other 36th move loses: the second-best scores about -6.7 for White.

sections.question: Suppose you cannot calculate every line after 36.Bf1 to the end. What makes the move safe to play anyway?
options: Every other move lost by force, so the one remaining move had to be played.
The bishop move wins the black queen by force in every line.
It leads to a known theoretical endgame.
sections.explanation: That is the elimination method. Against a pass Black mates; against the other active tries Black wins too (Stockfish: the second-best move is about -6.7 for White). The bishop move is the survivor, and you may play it before its last line is clear. (Kasparov did see 36...Rd2 37.Rd7! in advance, but the method does not require it.)

lessons.title: Intermediate moves and desperadoes
lessons.objective: Before any recapture, check for a forcing move to insert first; when a piece is lost anyway, make it take something before it goes.

sections.md:
Every exchange has a moment where players stop calculating: the automatic recapture. Intermediate moves and desperadoes live in that moment.

An intermediate move (in German, Zwischenzug) is a forcing move played before the expected recapture: a check, a capture or a threat that must be answered first. Then you recapture, on better terms.

A desperado is a piece that is lost anyway. Before it is taken, it takes something itself, best with check or with a new threat. When both sides have a piece en prise, the side to move decides who loses more.

Yusupov's chapter on desperadoes in Chess Evolution 3 and Aagaard's on intermediate moves give one habit. Before any recapture, ask three questions:

1. Is my piece lost anyway? Then what can it take first?
2. Is there a check or a bigger threat I can insert?
3. If I recapture now, what does my opponent insert?

Lasker–Napier, Cambridge Springs 1904, is a whole game of these questions. From move 13 to move 28 almost every piece is attacked.

sections.prompt: Lasker–Napier, move 14. White to play. Take the knight on d4. After Black takes back the pawn on d5, the white knight is attacked by the e5-pawn. Do not trade it: find the intermediate move.
sections.hint: The knight should move with a purpose. Which square brings it next to the black king?
sections.explanation: 14.Nxd4 Nxd5 15.Nf5! The knight goes towards the king instead of trading itself. Once the d5-knight moves, the queens face each other on the open d-file, and that prepares the next intermediate move. Stockfish: 15.Nf5 +1.0, 15.Nxd5 -0.3.

sections.prompt: Black played 15...Nxc3, attacking the white queen. Do not recapture on c3 yet. White to play: two intermediate moves.
sections.hint: The queens face each other. Take first, then check.
sections.explanation: 16.Qxd8! Rxd8 17.Ne7+ Kh8. Queen trade first, then a check: White gains two tempi while the c3-knight is still under attack. Stockfish: 16.Qxd8 +1.2; 16.Nh6+ -1.1 and 16.bxc3 -2.7.

sections.prompt: Move 22. Pieces hang everywhere: the f7-bishop attacks the e8-rook, the e4-knight attacks the c5-bishop, and the g7-bishop eyes b2. White to play.
sections.hint: When both sides have pieces en prise, take the most valuable thing first. Then answer Black's desperado with a threat of your own.
sections.explanation: 22.Bxe8! takes the rook. 22...Bxb2 is Black's desperado: a pawn with an attack on the a1-rook. 23.Rb1! moves the rook and attacks the bishop. Stockfish: 22.Bxe8 +1.9, 22.Bxh5 -0.3; 23.Rb1 +2.3, 23.Rc1 +0.5.

sections.question: Your knight is attacked by a pawn and cannot be saved. Which move do you look for first?
options: A retreat square, in case the pawn does not take.
A capture with the knight, ideally with check or a new threat, before the pawn takes it.
A second piece to defend the knight.
sections.explanation: That is the desperado. A doomed piece that takes a pawn with check has won a pawn and a tempo. A retreat is impossible by assumption, and a defender does not help against a pawn: the pawn still wins a piece for a pawn.

lessons.title: Imagination: the quiet move
lessons.objective: Look past the end of the forcing sequence for the quiet move that cuts a defence, takes a square or brings one more piece.

sections.md:
Forcing lines end. Most players calculate the checks and captures, stop, and judge what they see. Aagaard's chapter on imagination points at the move after the forcing sequence: a quiet move that cuts a defender's line, takes a flight square or brings one more piece.

Three kinds of quiet move to look for:

1. Interference: put a piece on the line between a defender and what it defends.
2. A king move in the attack: when the opponent has no checks, your king can join.
3. The quiet tightening move: no check, but the threat is mate and nothing parries it.

A quiet move is hard to see because it gives the opponent a free move. Before you reject it, ask what he can do with that move. If the answer is nothing useful, the quiet move is often the strongest.

Two classics follow. In Réti–Bogoljubov, New York 1924, a bishop steps between a rook and the square it guards. In Short–Timman, Tilburg 1991, the white king walks from g1 to g5 with the queens still on.

sections.prompt: Réti–Bogoljubov, New York 1924. White to play. The queen and the rook behind it attack the f8-bishop. After a check, its only defender will be the d8-rook. Find the check, then the quiet move.
sections.hint: After the check, put the bishop on the line between the d8-rook and f8.
sections.explanation: 24.Bf7+ Kh8 25.Be8!! The bishop cuts the d8-rook off from f8. 25...Rxe8 26.Qxf8+ Rxf8 27.Rxf8# and anything else loses the f8-bishop. Bogoljubov resigned. Stockfish: 25.Be8 +10.8, the next move only +0.03.

sections.caption: After 25.Be8!!: the bishop stands on the d8-rook's line to f8. The f8-bishop is now attacked twice and defended by nobody.

sections.question: Why could Short walk his king up the board with queens and rooks still on?
options: Black had no checks, and his pieces were tied to the defence of f7, g7 and the back rank.
Kings are always safe in the middlegame when the queens are on.
The white king was protected by its pawn shield on f2 and g2.
sections.explanation: A king walk is safe when the opponent cannot create a single threat against the king. Timman's pieces were tied to f7, g7 and the eighth rank. The pawns on f2 and g2 stayed behind, so they gave the king no cover at all.

modules.title: Attack and the initiative
modules.summary: The dynamic side of the middlegame through master games: the king caught in the centre, the pawn storm, the initiative and the positional exchange sacrifice.
modules.source: Yusupov, Boost Your Chess 3 (ch. 1 attacking the king in the centre, ch. 20 pawn storms, ch. 21 the initiative); Euwe & Kramer, The Middlegame, Book II (dynamic features: the initiative, the attack on the king); Marin, Learn from the Legends (Petrosian's exchange sacrifices); model games Deep Blue–Kasparov 1997, Tal–Portisch 1965, Spassky–Petrosian 1969, Capablanca–Bernstein 1911, Petrosian–Spassky 1966, AlphaZero–Stockfish 2018

lessons.title: Attacking the king in the centre
lessons.objective: Keep the enemy king in the centre and open lines to it before it can castle, even at the cost of material.

sections.md:
A king that has not castled by move 15 is a target, if you can open the centre before it escapes. Yusupov's chapter on the subject in Boost Your Chess 3 reduces the method to three steps:

1. Stop castling. Check the king, pin a piece, or control the squares it needs (f8 and g8, or d8 and c8).
2. Open the centre. The e- and d-files are the roads to the king. A pawn break, or a piece sacrifice on e6, d5 or f7, removes the last shield.
3. Bring every piece. Each move should add an attacker or gain a tempo with a threat. A slow move gives the king time to run.

Material is secondary while the king is stuck. A sacrifice that keeps the king in the centre for five moves is often worth more than the piece. The danger runs the other way too: if the attack stops, the extra material decides.

Two models follow: Deep Blue's knight sacrifice against Kasparov in 1997, and Tal's rook sacrifice against Portisch in 1965.

sections.prompt: Deep Blue–Kasparov, game 6, New York 1997. White to play. Black's last move, 7...h6, attacks the g5-knight. Black has not castled. Find the sacrifice that keeps the king in the centre.
sections.hint: Do not retreat. Which square next to the black king can the knight take on, with an attack on the queen?
sections.explanation: 8.Nxe6! The knight takes a pawn and attacks the queen and the f8-bishop. Kasparov played 8...Qe7 9.O-O fxe6 10.Bg6+ Kd8; his king never castled and he resigned on move 19. Stockfish: 8.Nxe6 +1.2, the retreat 8.Ne4 +0.2.

sections.prompt: Tal–Portisch after 16.Rxe6+ fxe6 17.Qxe6+ Kf8. White is a rook down for two pawns. Find the move that keeps the attack alive.
sections.hint: Every white piece must join with a threat. One piece has not moved yet.

sections.question: What did the rook sacrifice 16.Rxe6+ achieve?
options: It won material by force.
It took away castling, opened the e-file and kept the king in the centre, at the cost of a rook for two pawns.
It forced a draw by perpetual check.
sections.explanation: After 16.Rxe6+ fxe6 17.Qxe6+ Kf8 the king can never castle, and the e-file is open. Stockfish rates the sacrifice as level (0.00) with perfect defence, so it did not win by force; at the board the defence proved too hard, and Portisch resigned on move 27. That is the trade-off of attacking a central king: the material is gone for good, the attack has to be fed.

lessons.title: Pawn storms and opposite-side castling
lessons.objective: When the kings stand on opposite wings, open lines with pawns faster than the opponent and count every tempo.

sections.md:
With the kings on opposite wings, both sides can throw pawns at the enemy king without weakening their own. The game becomes a race. Yusupov's chapter on pawn storms gives its rules:

1. Count tempi. Your storm matters only if it opens a file before the other side's storm does.
2. Pawns open lines; pieces mate. Push the pawn that will hit a pawn in front of the king (g4-g5 against ...h6, f4-f5 against ...e6), then put rooks on the opened file.
3. A pawn given to open a file is cheap. A tempo spent winning a pawn may lose the race.
4. Defend only when you must. One defensive move can cost the whole attack.

lessons.title: The initiative
lessons.objective: Keep the right to make threats: prefer the forcing move over the move that grabs material, and convert the initiative before it runs out.

sections.md:
Euwe and Kramer split the middlegame into static features (material, pawn structure, weak squares) and dynamic ones. The first dynamic feature is the initiative: the power to make threats the opponent must answer.

The initiative is a temporary asset. Each threat buys one move. When the threats stop, the opponent regroups and the static features decide again. So the side with the initiative must:

1. Prefer moves with threats to moves without them, even at the cost of a pawn.
2. Aim the threats where the opponent is weakest, so the answers are passive.
3. Convert in time: turn the initiative into something that lasts, such as material, a broken king position or a passed pawn.

The defender does the reverse: ignore threats that are not real, and win a tempo back whenever possible.

lessons.title: The positional exchange sacrifice
lessons.objective: Give a rook for a minor piece when the minor piece gets a square the rook can never contest and the position stays closed.

sections.md:
The exchange sacrifice gives a rook for a minor piece. Petrosian made it a positional weapon: he gave the exchange not for a mating attack but for squares, for a blockade, or to remove the opponent's best piece. Marin's Learn from the Legends gives Petrosian's exchange sacrifices a chapter of their own.

When does it pay?

1. The minor piece you get, or keep, has a strong square that the opponent's rook cannot challenge.
2. The rook you give up has no open file to work on.
3. The opponent's remaining pieces are passive, or his king becomes weak.
4. A pawn comes with it, and the position stays closed.

Rooks need open files. While the position stays closed and your minor piece dominates, a rook can be worth less than a knight.

Two games follow: Petrosian–Spassky, World Championship 1966, game 10, and AlphaZero–Stockfish (published 2018), where the program gave a rook for a knight to lock the black king in a dark-square bind.

lessons.title: Static and dynamic advantages
lessons.objective: Sort every advantage into static or dynamic, and let that decide whether you may wait or must act now.

sections.md:
Euwe and Kramer's The Middlegame is built on one division.

Static features change slowly: material, pawn structure, weak squares, the bishop pair, a passed pawn, a piece on an outpost that nothing can remove.

Dynamic features change every move: a lead in development, the initiative, a king caught in an open position, piece activity that depends on threats.

The division decides the plan.

- If your advantages are static, you can wait. Stop counterplay, trade the right pieces, and let the weakness or the extra pawn decide later.
- If your advantages are dynamic, act now. Open lines, make threats, and convert before the opponent completes his development or closes the position.

Yusupov's chapter on static advantages in Chess Evolution 3 adds the defender's view: against a dynamic advantage, survive the next few moves; against a static one, look for activity at once, because waiting only lets it grow.

lessons.title: Hanging pawns
lessons.objective: Judge hanging pawns by their mobility: push one when the advance opens a line, and attack them by forcing an advance that leaves a hole.

sections.md:
Hanging pawns are two pawns side by side on half-open files, usually on c5 and d5 (or c4 and d4), with no friendly pawns beside them. They come from the Queen's Gambit, the Queen's Indian and the Nimzo-Indian.

Their strength is dynamic. They control four central squares, and either one can advance. The push ...d4 or ...c4 opens lines for the pieces behind it at the moment it happens.

Their weakness is static. No pawn can defend them. If one advances too early, the other is left backward or isolated, and a blockader on the square in front of them fixes both.

Yusupov's chapter in Boost Your Chess 3 gives the plans:

- With the pawns: keep pieces on, support the pawns with rooks and queen, and push when the push opens a line or hits a piece.
- Against them: trade pieces, press them from the c- and d-files, and force an advance that leaves a hole.

lessons.title: Pawn majorities
lessons.objective: Use a pawn majority to make a passed pawn: in the centre to gain space and open lines, on the wing to create an outside passed pawn for the endgame.

sections.md:
A majority is a group of pawns that outnumbers the opponent's pawns on that part of the board: three against two on the queenside, or two against one in the centre. Yusupov gives each kind a chapter in Boost Your Chess 3.

A central majority is a middlegame weapon. Advanced with support, it gains space, drives enemy pieces from their squares and opens lines towards the king. Its danger: pushed too early or without support, the pawns become targets.

A queenside majority is an endgame weapon. It produces an outside passed pawn, far from the kings, which pulls the enemy king away while your king eats the pawns on the other wing.

Two rules for any majority:

1. The candidate moves first. The candidate is the pawn with no enemy pawn on its file; it is the one that will become passed.
2. Support before you push. A pawn that advances alone is blockaded and lost.

modules.title: Prophylaxis and defence
modules.summary: Think about the opponent's plan before your own, defend by counterattack, give or take material on purpose, and steer for fortresses.

lessons.title: Prophylactic thinking
lessons.objective: Before choosing a move, ask what your opponent wants to do, and prefer the move that improves your position and stops his plan.

sections.md:
Dvoretsky's prophylactic thinking is one habit: before you choose your move, ask what your opponent wants to do, and how you can stop it. Nimzowitsch called the result prophylaxis; Petrosian and Karpov built careers on it.

Ask the question in two forms:

1. What is his threat? That is defence, and every player does it.
2. What is his plan, if he had a free move? That is prophylaxis: you stop the plan before it becomes a threat.

Aagaard turns this into three training questions for quiet positions:

- Where are the weaknesses, his and mine?
- Which is my worst piece?
- What is my opponent's idea?

The answers point to the move: improve the worst piece to a square where it also stops his idea, or attack a weakness in a way that leaves him nothing useful to do. A player without useful moves soon makes harmful ones.

Karpov–Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974, is the purest example. Most of Karpov's moves take something away from Black rather than threaten something.

lessons.title: Defence and counterattack
lessons.objective: Meet a wing attack with a counterattack where the attacker's pieces are not, and find the only moves when there is no time to wait.

sections.md:
Defence is not waiting. Yusupov's chapters on defence, counterplay and counter-attack in Boost Your Chess 3 give the defender three tools, in order of preference:

1. Counterattack where the attacker is not. If his pieces are committed to one wing, his other wing and his king are short of defenders. A counter-threat that must be answered stops the attack for a move, and often for good.
2. Give material back. A pawn or the exchange returned at the right moment breaks the attack's momentum.
3. Simplify. Every exchange of an attacking piece reduces the danger; the queen is the first piece to trade.

Two errors to avoid: passive defence that lets the attacker bring one more piece, and panic, a sacrifice made before you have checked whether the threat is real.

Geller–Euwe, Zürich 1953, is the classic. Geller's queen has broken into h7 and his rook stands on h4. Euwe gives a rook to bring his own rook to the second rank, and his attack arrives first.

lessons.title: Material in defence: give it, or take it
lessons.objective: Give material back when it destroys the attacker's main asset, and accept a sacrifice when you have calculated that the attack is not decisive.

sections.md:
The defender's relation to material runs both ways.

Giving it back. When the attacker's play depends on one piece, one file or one pawn chain, the defender can give the exchange or a pawn to destroy it. Petrosian's 25...Re6!! against Reshevsky is the model: a rook for a bishop, so that a knight can blockade the centre for good. The material is not lost; it is spent on a static asset.

Taking it. When the opponent sacrifices, take if you have calculated that the attack is not decisive. Capablanca, against Marshall's prepared gambit in New York 1918, took the pawn and then the piece, and defended accurately. Refusing a sacrifice out of fear gives the attacker the initiative for free.

The test in both cases comes from Euwe and Kramer's split between static and dynamic. What will the position look like in ten moves? If his attack will have burnt out and your material remains, take. If his attack will grow and your extra material cannot help, give it back and change the character of the game.

lessons.title: Fortresses
lessons.objective: Recognise a fortress before you reach it, steer for it even at a cost, and hold it by keeping the king and pieces on the squares that close the entry.

sections.hint: Run for the corner, and take the route that the white king cannot cut.
sections.explanation: 1...Kg8! and the king reaches h8. The bishop can never control h8, so the king cannot be driven out: a fortress. Every other move loses (tablebase); for example 1...Kf8? 2.Kh7! and the king never gets to g8 or h8.

The white king cannot reach the h-file.
The h-pawn cannot pass the g7-square.
sections.explanation: The promotion square h8 is dark and the bishop moves on light squares. White can take g8 and g7 away, but then the black king shuttles on h8 and h7, or it is stalemate. With a dark-squared bishop the same position is an easy win.

lessons.objective: Play knight endings like pawn endings: activate the king, value the outside passed pawn, and know the knight check that stops a pawn on the seventh.

sections.md:
Botvinnik said that knight endings are pawn endings. The same factors decide: the active king and the passed pawn. A knight is a short-range piece; it cannot watch both wings at once. Yusupov's chapter on knight endings in Boost Your Chess 3 adds four points:

1. An outside passed pawn is even stronger than in a pawn ending: the knight that stops it is out of play.
2. A knight cannot lose a tempo. It needs an even number of moves to return to a square, so zugzwang is common.
3. Against a far-advanced pawn, the lone knight draws if it can reach a square in front of the pawn, or give a check that also covers the promotion square.
4. Rook pawns are the knight's worst enemy: in the corner it has only two squares.

Dvoretsky's key positions for knight against pawn come down to one geometry. A knight on d3 checks a king on b2 and covers c1. A knight on d2 checks a king on b3 and covers b1. Learn both.

sections.caption: The key geometry: the knight on d3 checks the king on b2 and covers c1, the promotion square. One move does both jobs, so the pawn cannot advance this turn.

sections.prompt: White to play. The b-pawn is one step from promotion and the white king is far away. Only one move draws.
sections.hint: Find the knight check that also covers b1.
sections.explanation: 1.Nd2+! checks the king on b3 and covers b1. After 1...Kc3 2.Nb1+ the knight keeps checking or blocking; the pawn never queens. Every other move loses (tablebase). Stockfish: 1.Nd2+ -0.4, a tablebase draw; 1.Kg4 -5.0.

sections.prompt: White to play. Stop the c-pawn with the knight and hold the draw.
sections.tip: Start with the check that covers c1 (Nd3+). Then keep the knight on squares that attack c1, or check the king whenever it guards c1. If the pawn promotes, the knight must be able to take it.

sections.question: Why are knight endings called "pawn endings" (Botvinnik)?
options: Because the same factors decide them: king activity and passed pawns, since a knight cannot cover both wings.
Because the knights are usually traded at once.
Because a knight is worth about one pawn in the endgame.
sections.explanation: A knight moves slowly and covers a small area. So an active king that eats pawns, and a passed pawn far from the knight, decide the game, exactly as in a king-and-pawn ending. The knight stays worth about three pawns; it just cannot be in two places.

lessons.title: Opposite-coloured bishops
lessons.objective: Know when opposite-coloured bishops draw (blockade on the defender's colour) and when they win (distant passed pawns, an active king), and use the king above material.

sections.md:
With bishops of opposite colours, the defender's king and bishop can blockade pawns on squares the attacker's bishop never controls. Even two extra pawns are often a draw. Dvoretsky's chapter on these endings and Yusupov's in Build Up Your Chess 3 give the rules:

1. Connected passed pawns are stopped by the king in front of them, on the squares the defending bishop controls.
2. Two passed pawns win when they are far apart, as a rule with at least two files between them: the king stops one, and the bishop cannot stop the other and guard everything else.
3. The attacker needs his king. The bishop alone cannot force pawns past a blockade.
4. The defender puts his king in front of the most dangerous pawn and uses his bishop on a long diagonal against the other.

Topalov–Shirov, Linares 1998, shows rule 3 in its most extreme form. Black has passed pawns on a4 and d5. To bring his king to e4 and d3, Shirov gives his bishop away.

sections.question: With opposite-coloured bishops, which pair of extra passed pawns gives the best winning chances?
options: Pawns far apart, such as on the a- and d-files.
Connected pawns, such as on the d- and e-files.
Doubled pawns on one file.
sections.explanation: Connected pawns can be stopped by the king on the defending bishop's colour, with the bishop guarding the other square. Pawns far apart split the defence: the king can stop one, the bishop must stop the other, and the attacking king breaks through on one side.

lessons.title: Queen endings
lessons.objective: Win queen endings with the cross-check and the passed pawn, and save them with perpetual check.

sections.md:
Queen endings are the longest and most tactical endings in chess. The last chapter of Yusupov's Chess Evolution 3 and Dvoretsky's chapter on queen endgames reduce them to four ideas:

1. The passed pawn counts more than material: how far it has advanced matters more than how many pawns each side has.
2. Centralise the queen. From the centre it stops the pawn, guards its own king and checks in every direction.
3. The defender's main weapon is perpetual check. The attacker's king needs shelter, often in front of his own pawn or near the enemy pawns.
4. The cross-check: answer a check by putting your queen in the way, with check of your own. If he trades queens, the pawn ending decides; if he does not, you win his queen.

Drill the cross-check and the perpetual. The first wins queen endings, the second saves them.

sections.prompt: White to play. The black queen checks on the h-file. Escape with a check of your own.
sections.hint: Which square on the h-file blocks the check and attacks the king on b8?
sections.explanation: 1.Qh2+! blocks the check and gives check along the h2-b8 diagonal: a cross-check. 1...Qxh2+ 2.Kxh2 and the f-pawn is outside the black king's square: f7 and f8 follow. A king move instead loses the queen to Qxh8. Stockfish: 1.Qh2+ wins; 1.Kg2 Qxf6 is a draw.

sections.caption: Black to move. White threatens b8=Q. Black checks from f2 and f1 in turn: the white king can only go between h1 and h2, and the white queen cannot block on g1 or g2.

sections.prompt: Black to move. Give perpetual check before the b-pawn queens.
sections.tip: Start with Qf2+. The king has only h1 and h2: check on f1 when it goes to h1, and on f2 when it goes to h2. The white queen cannot block on g1 or g2.

sections.question: Your king is in check from the enemy queen. You block with your own queen and give check at the same time. What is this called, and what does it force?
options: A cross-check: the opponent must trade queens or lose his queen.
A skewer: it wins a rook behind the king.
A stalemate trick: it forces a draw.
sections.explanation: The cross-check is the main winning tool in queen endings. It ends the opponent's checks at once, and the resulting pawn ending (or the extra queen) decides. Before you enter it, count the pawn ending.

lessons.title: Realising an advantage
lessons.objective: Convert a winning position by method: do not hurry, activate the king, create a second weakness, and break through only when everything is ready.

sections.md:
Yusupov's chapter on realising an advantage and Shereshevsky's Endgame Strategy agree on the method. A won position is not won until the technique is right.

1. Do not hurry. If the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece before you act.
2. Activate the king. In the endgame it is a strong piece.
3. Two weaknesses. One weakness can be defended. Attack a second one on the other wing, and the defender's pieces cannot cover both.
4. Trade the right pieces: his active ones, not yours.
5. Calculate the transition. A pawn ending or a pure rook ending must be checked to the end before you go into it.

Two models. In Capablanca–Tartakower, New York 1924, Capablanca lets two pawns go to bring his king to f6. In Carlsen–Karjakin, World Championship 2016, game 10, Carlsen makes fifty moves of small improvements before he breaks through with 57.b5.

sections.question: Which principle explains Capablanca's 35.Kg3, which let Black win two pawns?
options: King activity: in a rook ending, a king supporting the rook on the seventh and a passed pawn is worth more than two pawns.
When ahead in material, trade pieces, not pawns.
Rooks belong behind passed pawns.
sections.explanation: Capablanca was not ahead in material after 37...Rxf4+; he was two pawns down. What he had was activity: the king on f6, the rook on h7 and the pawn on g6 made threats Black could not meet, and the material came back with interest.
